basic_information.name: Executive Order 14110 — Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence
basic_information.effective_date: Signed October 30, 2023; published in Federal Register November 1, 2023 (88 FR 75191); revoked January 20, 2025 by EO 14148, replaced January 23, 2025 by EO 14179

scope_and_content.summary: The most sweeping US executive action on AI, EO 14110 established a government-wide framework for governing AI development and deployment through eight guiding principles covering safety, equity, civil rights, consumer protection, privacy, innovation, worker support, and international leadership. It used existing legal authorities — notably the Defense Production Act — to compel reporting from developers of the most powerful AI models (dual-use foundation models) and directed over 50 federal agencies to take more than 150 specific actions on deadlines ranging from 90 to 365 days.
key_provisions: Defined 'dual-use foundation models' as AI models trained on broad data using self-supervision, containing tens of billions of parameters, applicable across wide contexts, and exhibiting or potentially exhibiting high-level performance at tasks posing serious risk to security, health, or safety (e.g., CBRN weapon design, cyberattack facilitation, evasion of human control)
Set compute threshold at 10^26 floating-point operations (FLOPs) for models subject to mandatory reporting — at the time of signing, this exceeded any model trained to date

Invoked Defense Production Act (DPA) Title VII to compel developers of dual-use foundation models to notify the federal government when training such models and share results of red-team safety tests, cybersecurity measures, and model weight ownership information

Directed NIST to develop: (a) guidelines and best practices for AI red-teaming; (b) a companion resource to the AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) for generative AI; (c) a companion to the Secure Software Development Framework for generative AI and dual-use foundation models; (d) AI auditing and evaluation guidelines focused on cybersecurity and biosecurity
Required the Department of Commerce to develop guidance for watermarking and content authentication of AI-generated content (text, images, audio, video) to combat synthetic content and deepfakes

Directed Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) to propose regulations requiring US IaaS (Infrastructure-as-a-Service) providers to verify identities of foreign persons obtaining IaaS accounts — Know Your Customer (KYC) rules for cloud compute

Required agencies to address AI-related risks to critical infrastructure (energy, transportation, telecommunications, financial services, healthcare) in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security and sector-specific agencies
Established AI safety and security board within DHS for critical infrastructure AI governance
Directed HHS to develop an AI assurance policy for healthcare, establish an AI safety program, and develop a strategy for regulating AI use in drug development and healthcare delivery
Instructed DOJ and federal civil rights offices to combat algorithmic discrimination and ensure AI does not perpetuate unlawful bias in housing, lending, employment, and criminal justice
Directed agencies to attract and retain AI talent, including streamlining visa processes for AI specialists and establishing AI hiring programs across the federal workforce
Called for development of AI privacy protections, including evaluating how agencies collect and use commercially available data containing personal information
Promoted AI competition and innovation, including directing the SBA and NSF to support AI research at small businesses and startups
Directed US engagement with international allies and organizations (G7, OECD, UN) to establish common AI safety standards and ethical frameworks
scope_and_content.risk_classification: No formal tiered risk classification system (unlike the EU AI Act). Instead, the EO focused on a compute-based threshold approach: models trained using more than 10^26 FLOPs (or biological sequence models using more than 10^23 FLOPs) triggered mandatory reporting obligations. This threshold was designed to capture only the most capable frontier models. Below this threshold, the EO relied on sector-specific agency guidance rather than a unified risk taxonomy.
scope_and_content.covered_entities: Companies developing or demonstrating intent to develop dual-use foundation models exceeding the compute threshold; US IaaS providers (cloud infrastructure); federal agencies (over 50 agencies received directives); government contractors using AI. The EO did not directly regulate end-users or deployers of AI systems in the private sector — its authority over private companies was limited primarily to reporting and transparency requirements under the DPA.
scope_and_content.sector_scope: Cross-cutting federal government-wide scope, with sector-specific directives for: healthcare and drug development (HHS); education (Department of Education); housing and lending (HUD, CFPB); criminal justice and law enforcement (DOJ); critical infrastructure (DHS); national security and defense (DOD, intelligence community); labor and employment (Department of Labor); immigration (State Department visa processing); financial services (Treasury); transportation; and energy. Military and intelligence AI systems were addressed but through separate classified annexes and existing authorities.
scope_and_content.open_source_treatment: The EO directed the NTIA (National Telecommunications and Information Administration) to produce a report on dual-use foundation models with widely available model weights (i.e., open-weight/open-source models). The resulting NTIA report (published July 2024) recommended that the government 'actively monitor for potential risks but refrain from restricting the availability of open model weights for currently available systems.' The EO itself did not create explicit exemptions for open-source models from reporting requirements — the 10^26 FLOP threshold applied regardless of whether model weights were released publicly. However, the NTIA report's recommendation signaled a policy preference against restricting open-weight models, and the practical effect was that most open-source models at the time fell below the compute threshold.
scope_and_content.extraterritorial_reach: Limited extraterritorial reach compared to the EU AI Act. The EO's core mechanism — DPA-based reporting requirements — applied to companies developing models within US jurisdiction. The IaaS KYC provision had some extraterritorial implications, requiring US cloud providers to verify identities of foreign customers. However, the EO could not directly compel compliance from non-US companies operating outside US territory. Indirect extraterritorial effects existed through: (a) US cloud infrastructure dominance (most frontier model training runs on US cloud), making the IaaS rules globally impactful; (b) the US government's ability to condition market access and government contracts on compliance.

compliance_and_enforcement.penalties: The EO itself did not create new penalty structures. Enforcement relied on existing legal authorities: (1) Defense Production Act Title VII: willful failure to comply with reporting requirements is punishable by up to $10,000 fine and/or up to 1 year imprisonment per violation; the government can also seek court injunctions to enforce compliance; (2) Federal agencies could use existing regulatory authorities within their domains to enforce sector-specific directives; (3) Government contracting sanctions — non-compliant companies could face suspension or debarment from federal contracts. In practice, the DPA penalties were modest compared to EU AI Act fines, and no enforcement actions were publicly initiated before the EO's revocation.
compliance_and_enforcement.enforcement_body: No single dedicated enforcement body was created. Enforcement was distributed across existing agencies: Department of Commerce (via BIS) for reporting requirements and IaaS KYC rules; NIST for standards development (advisory, not enforcement); individual sector agencies (HHS, DOJ, DHS, etc.) for their respective directives; Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for government AI use policies; White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) for coordination. The AI Safety Institute within NIST was established to evaluate frontier models but had advisory rather than enforcement authority.
compliance_and_enforcement.compliance_timeline: Aggressive phased timeline with 150+ actions across multiple deadlines: 90 days (by late January 2024) — 21 requirements including initial NIST guidelines, DPA reporting framework setup, and initial agency AI assessments (White House claimed all 21 completed; independent verification confirmed only 11 of 21 = 52%); 180 days (by late April 2024) — 69 requirements including IaaS KYC rule proposal, DHS AI safety board establishment, and healthcare AI strategy (independent verification: 49 of 69 = 71% completed); 270 days (by late July 2024) — NIST guidelines and best practices for trustworthy AI, energy sector AI standards; 365 days (by October 2024) — remaining agency actions, comprehensive reports. BIS proposed its formal reporting rule in September 2024, with a 30-day response requirement once companies received questions. The entire framework was revoked before many deadlines were reached or rules finalized.
compliance_and_enforcement.reporting_requirements: Companies developing dual-use foundation models (above 10^26 FLOP threshold) were required to: (1) notify the federal government when beginning to train such models; (2) share results of red-team safety tests conducted per NIST guidelines; (3) report physical and cybersecurity measures protecting model weights; (4) disclose model weight ownership and access controls; (5) report on model capabilities, limitations, and potential misuse vectors. BIS proposed quarterly reporting cadence. Upon receiving a notice of applicable activities, BIS would issue specific questions to the reporting entity, which had 30 calendar days to respond. Federal agencies themselves had extensive internal reporting requirements: annual AI use inventories, risk assessments, and compliance reports to OMB.
compliance_and_enforcement.sme_provisions: Limited specific SME provisions compared to the EU AI Act. The EO directed the SBA (Small Business Administration) to support AI innovation at small businesses, and NSF to fund AI research at smaller institutions. The 10^26 FLOP compute threshold effectively exempted all but the largest companies from DPA reporting requirements — at the time of signing, only a handful of companies (primarily OpenAI, Google/DeepMind, Anthropic, Meta, and a few others) had the resources to train models at that scale. The NIST AI Safety Institute was directed to provide resources and guidance that would be accessible to smaller developers. However, the EO did not include formal regulatory sandbox provisions, reduced compliance fees, or structured support mechanisms specifically for startups in the way the EU AI Act does.

impact_and_analysis.business_impact: LARGE ENTERPRISES (frontier AI labs): The most significant impact fell on the 5-10 companies capable of training models above the 10^26 FLOP threshold — primarily OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, and Inflection AI. These companies faced DPA-mandated reporting obligations but many were already conducting voluntary safety testing and red-teaming. The compliance burden was moderate relative to their resources. STARTUPS AND SMEs: Minimal direct regulatory burden due to the high compute threshold, which effectively excluded all but the largest labs. Indirect effects included: (a) potential benefits from NIST safety standards that could reduce downstream liability risk; (b) access to government AI talent programs and SBA support; (c) positive signal for responsible AI development that could attract enterprise customers. CLOUD PROVIDERS: The IaaS KYC requirements created new compliance costs for AWS, Azure, GCP, and other cloud providers, requiring identity verification infrastructure for foreign customers. GOVERNMENT CONTRACTORS: Federal agencies' AI procurement and use guidelines created new market opportunities for AI companies selling to government but also imposed additional documentation and testing requirements.
impact_and_analysis.innovation_effect: Contested effects with strong partisan divide. CONSTRAINING arguments: (1) Chamber of Commerce and tech industry groups (NetChoice, SIIA, with members Amazon, Meta, Google) argued the EO threatened to hinder private sector innovation through burdensome reporting and government oversight; (2) Senator Ted Cruz called it 'barriers to innovation disguised as safety measures'; (3) The 10^26 FLOP threshold, while high, could quickly become binding as compute scales exponentially; (4) BIS quarterly reporting created administrative overhead for frontier labs. PROMOTING arguments: (1) The EO invested in AI research and talent (visa streamlining, NSF/SBA funding); (2) NIST safety standards could reduce uncertainty and lower barriers to responsible AI deployment; (3) Red-teaming requirements arguably improved model quality and safety; (4) International AI governance leadership could establish US companies as trusted AI providers globally. NET ASSESSMENT: The direct innovation constraint was narrow (only affecting a handful of frontier labs), but the signaling effect — that comprehensive regulation was coming — influenced investment decisions and corporate strategy more broadly.
impact_and_analysis.global_influence: Significant influence as the most comprehensive AI governance action by any major country at the time of signing (October 2023). INTERNATIONAL EFFECTS: (1) Influenced the UK AI Safety Summit (November 2023) and Bletchley Declaration, with many countries citing the US EO as inspiration; (2) The G7 Hiroshima AI Process and OECD AI governance discussions were shaped by EO 14110 provisions; (3) Established the US AI Safety Institute as a counterpart to the UK AI Safety Institute, creating a bilateral safety testing framework; (4) Influenced the EU AI Act's final negotiations (completed December 2023), particularly on GPAI model safety testing; (5) Provided a template for countries considering AI governance measures. LIMITATIONS: (1) As an executive order rather than legislation, it was inherently fragile — demonstrated by its rapid revocation; (2) The revocation sent an international signal that US AI policy is unstable across administrations; (3) Post-revocation, US global credibility on AI safety governance diminished, potentially accelerating other countries' independent regulatory efforts.
impact_and_analysis.stakeholder_positions: SUPPORTERS: Democratic members of Congress — Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Rep. Ted Lieu (D-CA), Rep. Don Beyer (D-VA, House AI Caucus leader) praised it as 'comprehensive strategy for responsible innovation'; Civil rights organizations — ACLU praised anti-discrimination provisions; Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights CEO Maya Wiley praised fairness provisions while urging congressional action; AI safety community — organizations like the Center for AI Safety and Partnership on AI generally supported the safety testing framework; Some industry players — Microsoft and Google publicly expressed support for responsible AI governance (while their trade associations expressed concerns). CRITICS: Republican members of Congress — Sen. Ted Cruz called it 'barriers to innovation disguised as safety measures'; House Oversight Committee held hearings arguing reporting requirements were 'broad and overreaching' and would 'stifle US innovation'; Industry trade groups — Chamber of Commerce, NetChoice (Amazon, Meta, Google members), SIIA argued the EO hindered innovation; Open-source advocates — expressed concern that compute thresholds could eventually constrain open-weight model development; Libertarian-leaning organizations — George Washington University's Regulatory Studies Center warned of 'structural challenges' in the EO's ambitious timeline and agency coordination.
impact_and_analysis.deregulatory_signals: The EO itself was pro-regulation, but its fate illustrates the strongest deregulatory signal in global AI governance. Trump revoked EO 14110 on his first day in office (January 20, 2025) via EO 14148, then signed EO 14179 ('Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence') on January 23, 2025. The replacement order explicitly frames AI regulation as a barrier to American innovation and dominance. Specific deregulatory mechanisms: (1) Immediate revocation of all EO 14110 provisions; (2) Review and potential rescission of all policies, regulations, and directives created pursuant to EO 14110; (3) OMB directed to revise memoranda M-24-10 and M-24-18 (government AI use guidance); (4) 180-day AI Action Plan development with innovation-first philosophy; (5) No mention of safety testing, red-teaming, or reporting obligations; (6) Framing that AI systems should be 'free from ideological bias or engineered social agendas' — signaling retreat from equity/civil rights provisions. The BIS reporting rule was never finalized and is effectively dead. NIST AI Safety Institute continues to operate but with reduced mandate and uncertain future.

recent_developments: Jan 20, 2025: President Trump revoked EO 14110 via EO 14148 on his first day in office, effective immediately
Jan 23, 2025: Trump signed EO 14179 'Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence' as replacement, directing a 180-day AI Action Plan focused on innovation and deregulation
Jan-Feb 2025: Agencies began reviewing and suspending/rescinding actions taken pursuant to EO 14110; OMB directed to revise AI governance memoranda M-24-10 and M-24-18
Feb 2025: BIS reporting rule for dual-use foundation models (proposed September 2024) effectively abandoned, never finalized
Mar 2025: NIST AI Safety Institute continued operating but with reduced scope and uncertain mandate under new administration; several key staff departed

Jul 2025: Trump administration published 'America's AI Action Plan' — the replacement policy document focusing on maintaining US AI dominance through deregulation and public-private partnership rather than safety-focused oversight
2025-2026: Multiple US states advanced their own AI legislation (Colorado AI Act implementation, various state proposals) partly to fill the federal governance gap left by EO 14110 revocation
2025-2026: International partners (UK, EU, Japan, Canada) continued bilateral AI safety cooperation despite US federal policy shift, working with NIST AI Safety Institute on voluntary basis

teaching_relevance.entrepreneurial_implications: EO 14110 is a critical case study for AI entrepreneurs on three levels: (1) REGULATORY RISK: The rapid cycle of enactment (Oct 2023) and revocation (Jan 2025) — just 15 months — demonstrates that AI startups cannot rely on stable federal AI policy in the US; founders must build compliance strategies that are robust to policy reversals across administrations, a uniquely American challenge compared to the EU's legislative approach. (2) COMPUTE THRESHOLD DESIGN: The 10^26 FLOP threshold was deliberately set high enough to exempt all but the largest frontier labs, illustrating how regulatory design can either protect or burden startups — a useful contrast with the EU AI Act's broader scope. For entrepreneurs, this means understanding that the same regulatory concept (AI safety rules) can be implemented in ways that are startup-friendly or startup-hostile depending on thresholds and definitions. (3) STRATEGIC POSITIONING: The existence of EO 14110 (even after revocation) created lasting market dynamics — enterprise customers now expect AI vendors to demonstrate safety testing and responsible AI practices, regardless of legal requirements; safety and compliance became competitive differentiators. The compliance market itself became an opportunity — companies like Anthropic positioned safety-first messaging as a go-to-market advantage. (4) GOVERNMENT AS CUSTOMER: The EO directed federal agencies to adopt AI responsibly, creating a massive government AI procurement market; startups selling to government must understand that procurement rules may persist even after the parent EO is revoked. (5) INTERNATIONAL IMPLICATIONS: Startups operating globally cannot optimize for one jurisdiction — what the US deregulates, the EU may mandate; founders must factor multi-jurisdictional compliance into their business models from day one.

confidence.caveats: The EO has been formally revoked (January 20, 2025), making it a historical document rather than current law. However: (1) Many actions taken pursuant to the EO (NIST standards, agency guidelines) were not automatically nullified — agencies must individually review and rescind them; (2) The legal status of actions-in-progress at the time of revocation remains ambiguous for some provisions; (3) State-level AI legislation continues to evolve partly in response to the federal governance gap; (4) The BIS reporting rule was never finalized, so its exact requirements remain in proposed form only; (5) Implementation tracking data shows significant shortfalls — independent verification found only 52% of 90-day requirements and 71% of 180-day requirements were completed, suggesting the EO was aspirational in scope; (6) Some provisions (particularly around government AI use) may be partially preserved or modified rather than fully rescinded under the new administration.
